1. Heard the learned Counsel for the parties.

2. This is an application for pre-arrest bail in connection with CR No.9 of 2023 registered with CBD,
Belapur Police Station, Navi Mumbai, for the offfences punishable under Section 420 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 ("the Penal Code").
3. The first informant runs a restaurant.
Husband of the first informant became acquainted with Tejas Shetty (A1).
The first informant had placed an order to supply liquor and other material required to organize a party at the restaurant of the first informant.

A sum of Rs.2,00,000/- was Tejas Rameh Shetty And Anr vs State Of Maharashtra on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/137701507/

sentences.text: The applicant Tejas (A1) did not refund the said amount.
The cheques drawn by Tejas (A1) to repay the said amount were dishonored, thrice.

4. As the first informant was in need of FL3 licence, the applicant Tejas (A1) represented that he would arrange the liquor licence within a period of three to four months upon payment of Rs.18,00,000/-.

The first informant and her husband credited amounts in the account of Tejas (A1)
and Rupali (A2), the wife of Tejas.

By making a further false representation that a FL2 (wine shop)
licence would be obtained in the joint names of the applicant Tejas (A1) and the husband of the first informant, Tejas (A1) made them to transfer further amounts.
Sanjay Jangid (A3) was introduced by the accused as an officer of Excise Department.
On the instructions of Sanjay Jangid (A3) the first informant was made to incur expenditure for interior and other changes in the hotel to the tune of Rs.24,00,000/-.
Eventually, Tejas (A1) conceded that he had not processed any proposal for issue of liquor licence and deceived the first informant.
Tejas (A1) delivered two cheques.
One drawn on his account and another drawn on the account of Rupali (A2).
Those cheques were dishonored on presentment.
Hence, the report.

The learned Counsel for the applicant submitted that the substance of the allegations against the applicants is that the first informant had deposited a sum of Rs.37,63,946/- in the accounts of the applicants and the cheques drawn by the applicants towards repayment of the said amount have been dishonoured.
Complaints against the applicants for having committed the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, are already lodged.
Therefore, at this juncture, the custodial interrogation of the applicants is not warranted.
Hence, the applicants deserve to be released on pre-arrest bail.
6. The learned APP and the learned Counsel for the first informant resisted the prayer for pre-arrest bail.
7. I have carefully perused the allegations in the FIR and the material on record.
The case sought to be set up on behalf of the applicants in a rather oversimplistic manner cannot be readily acceded to.
It is true, failure to perform a promise is distinct from an offence of cheating.
On a mere failure to perform the promise an inference of cheating cannot be drawn.
To constitute cheating, it has to be shown that the intention of the accused was dishonest since the inception of the transaction.
In the case at hand, in my considered view, the necessary elements to draw such an inference of dishonest intention are evident.
Firstly, there is material to indicate that the amounts were credited to the accounts of the applicants through banking channels.

The learned Counsel for the applicants attempted to wriggle out of the situation by asserting that the applicant No.1 acted as middleman only and the said amounts were transferred to one Vinay, whom the applicants had appointed to procure the licences.

I am afraid, by simply asserting in the application for pre-arrest bail that the amount was, in turn, transferred to an agent, the applicants can be permitted to wriggle out of the Tejas Rameh Shetty And Anr vs State Of Maharashtra on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/137701507/
2 situation.

sentences.text: Secondly, the allegations in the FIR indicate that the applicant No.1 had executed writing acknowledging the liability.
Thirdly, the cheques drawn towards repayment were dishonored on presentment.
Fourthly, the nature of the transaction was such that it cannot be appraised on the premise of failure to perform the promise.
The underlying transaction had no semblance of legitimacy, to urge that it was a case of failure to prerform the promise.
The applicants were not holding the position to either procure or transfer the liquor licences.

Lastly, the intention to deceive becomes 4-ABA2292-2023.DOC prima facie evident from the manner in which the first informant was induced to part with huge amounts by making multiple false representations.

9. Custodial interrogation of the applicants is, therefore, warranted to unearth the fraud, unmask the identity of the persons who were privy to the fraud and also have the money trail, especially in the backdrop of the fact that the credit of huge amount to the accounts of the applicants through banking channel is prima facie evident.
I am, therefore, not inclined to exercise discretion in favour of the applicants.

10. Hence, the following order:
:ORDER:
(i) Application stands rejected.
(ii) It is clarified that these prima facie observations are confined to determine entitlement to pre-arrest bail only.
[N. J. JAMADAR, J.]
